[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal development showing how each step built on the last with precise examples.
Secure: Clear development with relevant examples.
Developing: Some development; balance uneven.
Emerging: Lists discoveries without causal links.

before.content_html:
The Wrong Theory That Almost Made Sense

For most of the 19th century educated British people believed disease came from miasma — bad air rising from rotting waste, sewage and stagnant water. Cholera in Soho? Bad air from the cesspits. Childbed fever in maternity wards? Bad air from the linen. Hospital wounds going septic? Bad air from open windows. Miasma theory was wrong, but it was coherent: it predicted that clean smells meant safe places, dirty smells meant dangerous ones. It even produced useful action — hospital ventilation, street cleaning, lime in graveyards. The problem was that the actual cause of disease was invisible, and miasma blocked the search for it.

Key Fact

In 1861 Louis Pasteur published his germ theory, proving that microscopic organisms (germs) caused decay and disease. He had been investigating fermentation for the French brewing and silk industries; the medical implications followed.

Pasteur and the Germ Theory of Disease

Louis Pasteur was a French chemist, not a doctor. The French wine and silk industries hired him in the 1850s to find out why their products were going bad. By using a microscope and a series of swan-necked flask experiments, Pasteur showed that microbes carried in the air caused fermentation and decay. He published this as the Germ Theory of Disease in 1861. By the 1880s he had extended the principle into a vaccine programme: chicken cholera (1879, by chance — an old culture left over a holiday weekend turned out to immunise rather than infect), anthrax (1881, in a famous public demonstration where vaccinated sheep survived and unvaccinated ones died) and rabies (1885, on a 9-year-old boy bitten by a rabid dog).

Koch and the Microbe Hunters

Pasteur proved germs caused disease in general. Robert Koch, a German country doctor, took the next step: identifying which germ caused which disease. Working alone in a converted darkroom and later in Berlin, Koch developed the techniques that made modern microbiology possible. He stained bacteria so they could be seen under a microscope. He grew them on agar jelly so colonies could be isolated. He photographed them so others could see what he saw. In 1876 he identified the anthrax bacterium. In 1882 he found the bacterium that causes tuberculosis — then the biggest killer in Britain. In 1883 he identified cholera. Koch was the first to fulfil the ‘one germ, one disease’ rule that became the basis of modern medicine.

Pasteur was French; Koch was German. The two countries had fought a war (Franco-Prussian, 1870-71) and the rivalry continued in their laboratories. When Koch identified TB in 1882, Pasteur responded with the rabies vaccine in 1885. When Pasteur produced anthrax vaccination in 1881, Koch attacked his methods publicly. National pride drove output: governments funded laboratories partly to outcompete the other side.

For the AQA factor essay this is a lovely example of how science, communication and the role of the individual interact. Without rivalry, the pace of discovery would have been slower; without good communication (scientific journals, photographs of bacteria), the results would not have spread.

Ehrlich and the ‘Magic Bullet’

Paul Ehrlich, a German researcher trained under Koch, took germ theory in a new direction. If specific bacteria caused specific diseases, perhaps specific chemicals could destroy specific bacteria without harming the patient. Ehrlich called this idea a magic bullet. After testing 605 compounds, the 606th — a compound of arsenic now called Salvarsan — cured syphilis. He published this in 1909. It was the first chemical cure for an infectious disease. The next leap came in 1932 when the German company Bayer introduced Prontosil, a sulphonamide drug effective against streptococcal infection. The age of chemotherapy had begun — though large-scale antibiotics would have to wait for penicillin in the 1940s.

Why Britain Lagged

Pasteur published in 1861. Lister applied germ theory to surgery in Britain in 1867. By the 1880s, Koch had identified specific bacteria. Yet many British doctors and public health officials clung to miasma well into the 1880s.

Training: medical schools had taught miasma for decades; doctors trained before 1860 saw no compelling reason to switch frameworks late in their careers. Visibility: nobody could see germs without a microscope, and decent microscopes were expensive and required expert use. Communication: French research took time to translate into English, and British scientific culture was suspicious of Continental theory after decades of intermittent war with France. The shift was generational — older doctors retired, younger doctors trained in the new framework, and miasma quietly disappeared from the textbooks by the early 1900s.

Key Fact

Robert Koch identified the bacteria causing anthrax (1876), tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883). His staining and culture techniques made systematic bacteriology possible. By 1900 the ‘one germ, one disease’ rule was the basis of modern medical thinking.

Everyday Medicine in the Age of Germ Theory

For ordinary people in Britain, germ theory’s practical effects took time to arrive. Doctors continued to prescribe traditional remedies — cod liver oil, beef tea, mustard plasters — alongside new advice on hygiene. Hospitals began to insist on hand-washing, instrument sterilisation and clean wards by the 1890s. Patent remedies still flooded the market: Beecham’s Pills, Carter’s Little Liver Pills, Bovril marketed as a tonic. The professional doctor was now scientifically grounded in a way that had been impossible in 1860, but the patient’s medicine cabinet still mixed old and new.

Linking to the Factor Essay

Germ theory is the cleanest example in the unit of science and technology as the dominant factor — without microscopes, staining and the new theoretical framework, none of this happens. But the lesson also shows the other factors at work. Communication: Pasteur and Koch published in scientific journals that crossed borders rapidly. The role of the individual: Pasteur, Koch and Ehrlich made discoveries that depended on personal genius and persistence. Government: French and German states funded laboratories; British government was slower. Chance: the 1879 chicken-cholera vaccine came from a forgotten flask. A factor-essay question naming ‘science and technology’ can be answered using this lesson alone, but the strongest answers reach across periods to compare the role of science here with its role in earlier eras (Vesalius, Harvey) where science was necessary but not sufficient on its own.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 16-mark factor essay, the most common slip is to write a paragraph on each factor without weighing them. The mark scheme rewards explicit comparison: ‘Science and technology was the dominant factor in the germ theory revolution because without the microscope and Pasteur’s experimental method none of the discoveries are possible. However, the role of the individual was also crucial — the rivalry between Pasteur and Koch drove the pace of discovery, and a less determined scientist might have failed where they succeeded. On balance science was necessary but the individual decided the pace.’ A sentence like that — comparison plus judgement — is what unlocks the top band.

lessons.title: A Revolution in Surgery: Anaesthetics and Antiseptics

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which surgery before 1846 and surgery after 1900 were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: pre-1846 surgery relied on speed because patients were conscious; post-1900 surgery used anaesthetics so operations could last hours.
• Difference: pre-1846 theatres were dirty and infection killed up to half of patients; post-1900 aseptic theatres used sterilised instruments, gowns and rubber gloves.
• Similarity: in both periods surgeons worked on amputations, tumours and trauma — the procedures continued, but the survival rates were transformed.
• Similarity: in both periods individual surgeons (Liston, Lister, Halsted) drove change through personal example.

[4 marks — 2 marks per comparison: 1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Joseph Lister for the development of surgery in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Lister’s 1865 use of carbolic acid on a compound fracture, published in The Lancet in 1867, cut amputation mortality from around 46% to 15% in his Glasgow ward.
• At the time: he applied Pasteur’s germ theory directly to surgery, providing the first practical antiseptic system.

• The First World War (1914–18) accelerated the spread of transfusion, X-rays, antisepsis and plastic surgery (Gillies at Sidcup) far faster than peacetime would have allowed.

before.content_html:
Surgery Before 1846: Speed Was Everything

Before anaesthetics, surgery in Britain was a last resort. Patients screamed; surgeons worked at speed because every second of pain risked shock. The London surgeon Robert Liston could amputate a leg in 28 seconds. Operations were limited to crisis cases — trauma, tumours visible on the surface, gallstones, amputations — because anything inside the body chest or abdomen meant near-certain death from pain, blood loss or infection. Most patients refused surgery until the alternative was definitely worse.

Key Fact

Three early anaesthetics changed surgery: nitrous oxide (Davy 1799), ether (Morton, Boston 1846) and chloroform (James Simpson, Edinburgh 1847). Simpson tested chloroform on himself and friends after dinner.

Simpson and Chloroform, 1847

James Simpson was an Edinburgh obstetrician searching for a better anaesthetic than ether, which irritated the lungs. In November 1847 he and two colleagues sniffed chloroform after dinner and woke up on the floor. Within days he was using it in childbirth. Chloroform was easier to administer and worked faster than ether, and it spread quickly across British surgery.

There was sharp opposition. Some clergy quoted Genesis 3:16 — ‘in sorrow shalt thou bring forth children’ — arguing that pain in childbirth was God’s will. Surgeons feared patients dying from the anaesthetic itself; in 1848 Hannah Greener, a 15-year-old, died under chloroform during a toenail operation. The objections were overcome partly by Queen Victoria, who used chloroform when she gave birth to Prince Leopold in 1853. Royal endorsement made chloroform respectable.

Anaesthetics encouraged surgeons to operate longer, deeper and on patients who would once have refused. But operating theatres were filthy. Surgeons wore unwashed coats stiff with old blood, used unsterilised instruments and worked in wards crowded with infected patients. Post-operative infection — gangrene, sepsis, ‘hospital fever’ — killed up to 50% of surgical patients. Surgeons called these years the ‘Black Period’: more operations, more deaths. Anaesthetics had solved the pain problem and exposed an infection problem the older system had hidden behind speed.

Lister and Carbolic Acid, 1865–1867

Joseph Lister was a Glasgow surgeon who read Pasteur’s germ theory in 1864. If germs in the air caused decay, Lister reasoned, they must also cause wound infection. Carbolic acid was already used to deodorise sewage in Carlisle. Lister tried it on a compound fracture in August 1865: he soaked dressings in carbolic and rinsed instruments and hands with carbolic solution. The wound healed without infection. He published his results in The Lancet in March 1867. Antiseptic surgery — killing germs during surgery — had begun.

Key Fact

Lister’s carbolic spray cut amputation deaths from around 46% to 15% in his Glasgow ward by 1869. Yet many British surgeons rejected his system into the 1880s — the spray was unpleasant, results were variable in untrained hands, and surgeons could not see the germs Lister claimed to be killing.

From Antiseptic to Aseptic Surgery

Lister’s carbolic system killed germs during surgery. By the 1890s a better idea had taken hold: stop germs reaching the wound in the first place. Aseptic surgery meant sterilising instruments in steam autoclaves (1880s), wearing surgical gowns and face masks, scrubbing hands before operating and using rubber gloves — introduced by William Halsted in Baltimore in 1894 after his nurse’s hands cracked from carbolic. By 1900 most British operating theatres were aseptic rather than antiseptic, and infection rates had fallen sharply.

Industrial-scale shrapnel wounds in the trenches forced surgical innovation. Röntgen’s X-rays (1895) became routine in field hospitals from 1914 to locate metal fragments. Blood transfusions, made possible by Karl Landsteiner’s identification of blood groups (1901), saved lives at the front by 1916. Surgeons learned to debride wounds — cut away dead tissue before infection set in. Plastic surgery began with Harold Gillies treating facial injuries at the Queen’s Hospital, Sidcup. War accelerated changes that peacetime medicine would have taken decades to adopt.

Linking to the Factor Essay

Anaesthetics and antiseptics show science and technology driving change — Pasteur’s germ theory was the precondition for Lister’s breakthrough, and chemistry produced the carbolic. The role of the individual matters too: Simpson and Lister both pushed personally against opposition. Religion resisted chloroform on biblical grounds. Chance appears in Simpson’s after-dinner experiment. War accelerated the spread of antiseptic and aseptic surgery from 1914. The strongest factor essays note that no single factor explains the whole story: science enabled it, individuals pushed it, religion slowed it, war broadcast it.

before.content_html:
The Sick Industrial City

Between 1801 and 1851 Britain’s urban population doubled. Manchester, Liverpool, Leeds and Birmingham filled with back-to-back terraces sharing one privy between dozens of families. There were no sewers, no refuse collection and no clean water. Wells lay metres from cesspits. Pigs ran in courtyards. Death rates in the worst slums reached 30 per 1,000 — double the rural figure. Yet government action was blocked by a powerful idea: laissez-faire, the Whig conviction that the state should leave individuals and businesses alone.

Key Fact

Britain suffered four major cholera epidemics in the 19th century: 1831–32 (around 52,000 deaths), 1848–49, 1853–54 and 1865–66. Each forced government to act a little more than the last.

Chadwick’s 1842 Report

Edwin Chadwick was a lawyer and Poor Law Commissioner who collected mortality statistics from across Britain. His 1842 Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population argued that bad housing caused poverty, not the reverse: sick workers could not earn, and disease cost ratepayers more than sanitation would. The report sold widely, but Parliament dragged its feet for six years until cholera returned in 1848.

The 1848 Public Health Act

The 1848 Public Health Act created a General Board of Health and allowed towns to set up local boards if death rates exceeded 23 per 1,000 or if 10% of ratepayers petitioned for one. The catch was that adoption was voluntary — adoptive, not compulsory. Many towns refused on grounds of cost; others adopted then dropped boards once cholera receded. Chadwick’s authoritarian style provoked a backlash and the General Board was abolished in 1858. The Act’s effect was real but limited.

When cholera struck Soho in August 1854, the London doctor John Snow mapped 578 deaths and saw they clustered around one pump in Broad Street. Snow persuaded the parish to remove the pump handle on 8 September; new cases stopped. He had proved cholera was waterborne — seven years before Pasteur’s germ theory and without a microscope. The General Board of Health rejected his findings; they preferred miasma. Snow’s evidence won over local officials but not the medical establishment until germ theory caught up in the 1860s.

The Great Stink and Bazalgette’s Sewers

In summer 1858 hot weather turned the Thames, by then an open sewer, into the ‘Great Stink’. Curtains soaked in chloride of lime hung in Parliament; MPs could not sit. Within weeks, Parliament voted £3 million for Joseph Bazalgette to build a sewer network for London. Eighty-two miles of main sewer, 1,100 miles of street sewer, four pumping stations — finished by 1865. When cholera returned in 1866 it killed thousands in unsewered districts but spared the West End and central London where Bazalgette’s system was working. Public health had a winner.

The 1875 Public Health Act

By 1875 three things had shifted. Germ theory had begun to displace miasma. The 1867 Reform Act had given working-class men in towns the vote, so MPs needed slum voters. And Disraeli’s Conservative government had made ‘sanitas sanitatum, omnia sanitas’ (sanitation is everything) a slogan. The 1875 Act made local authorities responsible for sewers, water, refuse, food inspection, slaughterhouses, building standards and notifiable diseases. It was compulsory, not adoptive. The same Parliament passed the Artisans’ Dwellings Act allowing slum clearance, the Sale of Food and Drugs Act, and the Rivers Pollution Prevention Act. Public health had moved from individual responsibility to state duty.

Key Fact

The 1875 Public Health Act made action compulsory across all local authorities, covering sewers, water, food, housing and notifiable disease. Combined with the 1875 Artisans’ Dwellings Act, it ended the laissez-faire era in British public health.

Linking to the Factor Essay

Public health is the cleanest case for government as the dominant factor — the 1848 and 1875 Acts could only be passed by Parliament. But government did not act alone. Communication mattered: Chadwick’s report, Punch cartoons, Mayhew’s London Labour and the London Poor and the press during the Great Stink built the political pressure. The role of the individual: Chadwick, Snow and Bazalgette each pushed reform forward. Science and technology: Snow’s map, Bazalgette’s engineering, eventually Koch’s bacteriology. Chance: a hot summer in 1858 forced Parliament to act. Strong factor essays note that government became the decisive driver only once the other factors had built the case.

before.content_html:
Nursing Before Nightingale

In early Victorian Britain nursing was untrained and disreputable. Hospital nurses were often drawn from poor or unemployed women; many drank heavily on the wards. Charles Dickens captured the popular image in Martin Chuzzlewit (1843) with Sairey Gamp, a nurse who turned up drunk to deliver babies and laid out the dead. Hospitals themselves were feared. Patients only entered when home care had failed; surgical wards were filthy; ventilation was poor; mortality was high. The nursing reformation began in religious orders — Catholic nursing sisters and the Anglican Sisters of Mercy — long before Florence Nightingale, but in Britain it was Nightingale who made secular nursing a respected profession.

Key Fact

At the Scutari military hospital in 1854 mortality was around 42% when Nightingale arrived; within six months it had fallen to roughly 2%. She used a polar-area ‘rose’ diagram to convey the data to Parliament — one of the earliest political uses of statistical graphics.

Crimea, 1854: The Scutari Effect

When the Times war correspondent W.H. Russell reported the squalor of British military hospitals in the Crimean War in 1854, public outrage forced the government to act. Florence Nightingale took 38 nurses to the Scutari Barrack Hospital in Constantinople. She found wounded men crammed into vermin-infested wards, sewage in the basement, and rats. Nightingale insisted on cleanliness, ventilation, separation of patients by disease, decent food and proper laundry. Mortality fell sharply. She returned to Britain a national hero in 1856 and used her fame to lobby for permanent reform. Mary Seacole, refused by the War Office despite her Caribbean medical experience, paid her own way and ran the ‘British Hotel’ near Balaclava, nursing soldiers under fire.

Nightingale was a trained mathematician. She invented the polar-area chart — later called the rose diagram — to show that more British soldiers in Crimea died from preventable disease than from enemy bullets. She presented her statistics to Lord Panmure and the 1857 Royal Commission on the Health of the Army. Statistics, not anecdotes, won the argument. Her command of data made her one of the first women elected to the Royal Statistical Society in 1858, and her methods gave hospital reform an evidence base that critics could not easily dismiss.

Notes on Nursing and Notes on Hospitals, 1859

In 1859 Nightingale published two short books that shaped Victorian nursing and hospital practice for decades. Notes on Nursing argued that nursing was a skilled profession with its own knowledge base — observation, hygiene, ventilation, diet, quiet, light. Notes on Hospitals advocated the pavilion plan: long wards with windows on both sides for cross-ventilation, separate buildings for different diseases, and high ceilings. The new St Thomas’ Hospital (rebuilt 1868–71 on the Thames opposite Parliament) followed her design.

The Nightingale Training School, 1860

Public donations to the ‘Nightingale Fund’ financed a training school for nurses at St Thomas’ Hospital, opened in 1860. Trainee nurses lived in supervised accommodation, attended lectures, completed ward placements and qualified after a year. By 1900 the model had spread across British hospitals and the colonies. Nursing became respectable middle-class work; matrons gained authority over wards. The 1858 Medical Act, by registering doctors, professionalised the medical hierarchy too. Nursing and medicine moved together towards regulated professions.

Key Fact

The pavilion plan kept patients in long, well-ventilated wards separated by disease, reducing cross-infection long before germ theory explained why. Combined with rigorous hand-washing and clean linen, it cut hospital mortality across Britain in the second half of the 19th century.

Mary Seacole and Her Belated Recognition

Mary Seacole’s contribution was acknowledged less in her own time. She published her autobiography Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands (1857), and her work near the Crimean front earned the affection of returning soldiers, but in Britain she was largely forgotten until the late 20th century. Her statue was erected outside St Thomas’ Hospital in 2016. The contrast with Nightingale shows how race, class and access to political networks shaped which reformers became household names.

The 1858 Medical Act created the General Medical Council and a register of qualified doctors, ending centuries of overlap between physicians, surgeons, apothecaries and quacks. Voluntary hospitals (funded by donations) and Poor Law infirmaries (funded by ratepayers) expanded across the country, and after 1867 specialist hospitals for children, women and tropical diseases multiplied. Hospital medicine, professional nursing and a registered medical workforce reshaped British healthcare in the second half of the 19th century.

Linking to the Factor Essay

Nightingale shows several factors interlocking. War created the Crimean crisis that gave her a public stage. The role of the individual was decisive: another nurse with the same crisis would not have produced Notes on Hospitals. Communication spread her statistics, books and hospital plans across Britain. Government backed her through the 1857 Royal Commission and bought into pavilion-plan design. The strongest factor essays note that Nightingale’s legacy depended on all four working at once — remove war, and there is no Scutari; remove communication, and her statistics never reach Parliament.

• Lloyd George, Churchill, Beveridge, Bevan, Nightingale, Lister and Bazalgette each shaped specific reforms.

Judgement: war repeatedly forced action by exposing the gap between Britain’s aspirations and its workforce’s health, but war alone did not legislate — communication built the case and government delivered the law. before.description: Booth, Rowntree, the Boer War and the Liberal reforms that put the state into welfare for the first time.
before.content_html:
Late-Victorian Britain Discovers Its Poor

By 1900 most middle-class Britons assumed poverty was a moral failure: drink, idleness, fecklessness. Two surveys overturned that assumption. Charles Booth, a Liverpool ship-owner, financed and led Life and Labour of the People in London (1889–1903). His investigators found 30.7% of Londoners lived below the poverty line. Seebohm Rowntree, a Quaker chocolate manufacturer in York, replicated the work in his own city in 1901. Poverty: A Study of Town Life showed 28% of York’s population in the same condition — not just London. Rowntree distinguished ‘primary’ poverty (income too low to meet basic needs) from ‘secondary’ (where some money was wasted). Combined, the two reports made it impossible to keep blaming the poor for being poor.

Key Fact

Four pressures combined to push the state into welfare: Booth’s 1889–1903 London survey (30.7% in poverty); Rowntree’s 1901 York study (28%); the Boer War (1899–1902), which rejected 40% of working-class recruits as unfit; and the 1906 Liberal landslide.

The Boer War Shock, 1899–1902

When Britain went to war in South Africa in 1899, recruiting officers in northern industrial cities turned away around 40% of volunteers as physically unfit. In Manchester the rejection rate exceeded 60%. The 1903 Inter-Departmental Committee on Physical Deterioration confirmed the problem and linked it to childhood undernourishment. The Boer War transformed welfare from a moral question (should we help?) into a security question (can we field an army?). National efficiency, not compassion, made reform politically irresistible.

The 1906 Liberal Landslide

The Liberals won 397 seats to the Conservatives’ 156 in January 1906. Henry Campbell-Bannerman became Prime Minister, succeeded by Asquith in 1908. Three figures drove reform from inside government: David Lloyd George (Chancellor from 1908), Winston Churchill (then a Liberal, President of the Board of Trade) and William Beveridge, the young civil servant who designed Labour Exchanges. The Liberals had no welfare manifesto in 1906 — the reform programme was assembled in office, partly to head off the rising Labour Party and partly because Booth, Rowntree and the Boer War had changed the climate.

Children: Free School Meals (Education (Provision of Meals) Act, 1906) and School Medical Inspections (1907) tackled the Boer War health concerns directly. The Children Act 1908 (the ‘Children’s Charter’) banned the sale of tobacco and alcohol to children and set up juvenile courts. Old people: the Old Age Pensions Act 1908 paid 5 shillings a week to single people over 70 with incomes below £21 a year — means-tested, non-contributory, ‘Lloyd George’s pension’. Workers: Labour Exchanges (1909) helped the unemployed find work. The Trade Boards Act (1909) set minimum wages in ‘sweated’ trades. The People’s Budget (1909) raised income and inheritance taxes to fund all this; the House of Lords blocked it, triggering the 1911 Parliament Act that ended their veto.

National Insurance, 1911

The flagship reform was the National Insurance Act 1911. Part I gave 13 million workers earning under £160 a year free GP care, sick pay (10 shillings a week for 26 weeks) and maternity benefits. Workers paid 4 pence a week, employers 3 pence and the state 2 pence — Lloyd George’s slogan was ‘ninepence for fourpence’. Part II covered unemployment in seven trades vulnerable to seasonal layoffs (building, shipbuilding, engineering and others), paying 7 shillings a week for up to 15 weeks. It was the first nationwide compulsory health and unemployment insurance in Britain.

Key Fact

The 1911 Act covered the worker, not the family. Wives, children, the elderly and the chronically sick were excluded from Part I. Part II covered only seven trades. The Liberal reforms were a partial, contributory step — the universal welfare state had to wait for Beveridge and Bevan after WWII.

Opposition and Limits

The reforms faced opposition from several directions. The British Medical Association feared the loss of private patient income; doctors threatened to boycott the panel system until generous fees were agreed. Conservatives in the House of Lords blocked the People’s Budget, forcing the constitutional crisis of 1909–11. Friendly societies that had previously sold health insurance feared losing members. The Labour Party criticised the contributory model as a regressive tax on the working class. Yet the reforms held: by 1914 free school meals reached over 150,000 children daily, pensions were paid to about 970,000 elderly people, and 13 million workers were enrolled in the new health scheme. The state had crossed a line it could not uncross.

Linking to the Factor Essay

The Liberal reforms show four factors interacting. Communication: Booth and Rowntree turned anecdote into evidence. War: the Boer War made fitness a national-security argument. Government: only the 1906 Liberal landslide could deliver this scale of legislation. The role of the individual: Lloyd George, Churchill and Beveridge each shaped the design. The strongest factor essays note the chain — communication built evidence; war built urgency; government built law — and that in earlier periods (1348, 1665) the same diseases of poverty produced no equivalent state response.

• Over time: his discovery was the foundation Florey and Chain developed into a usable drug from 1939 onwards.

practice_questions.text: Explain how penicillin was developed into a usable drug.
practice_questions.marks:

• WWII shortages drove Florey to the United States; deep-tank fermentation by US firms scaled production from milligrams to tonnes.
• By D-Day 1944, enough penicillin existed to treat Allied wounded; battlefield infection mortality fell sharply.
• Causal chain: chance + individuals + science + war → the first mass antibiotic.

practice_questions.text: ‘Chance has been the most important factor in modern medical breakthroughs.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh chance against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of chance as the main factor:
• Fleming 1928: contaminated mould plate produced penicillin.
• Pasteur 1879: a forgotten chicken-cholera culture weakened to give him the principle of attenuated vaccines.
• Paré 1530s: running out of cauterising oil forced him to use a soothing salve which worked better.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Fleming’s plate produced nothing usable; Florey and Chain made it a drug. Jenner deliberately tested cowpox in 1796.

Weighed against war:
• WWII funding and demand turned penicillin into a battlefield drug. WWI accelerated transfusion, X-rays and plastic surgery (Gillies).

Weighed against science and technology:
• Deep-tank fermentation and electron microscopy were what scaled and explained the breakthrough. Without germ theory, Lister’s 1867 antiseptic surgery had no scientific footing.

Judgement: chance opens doors but explains nothing. Across the medieval, early modern and modern periods accidental discoveries only became medicines when prepared minds, organised science, war and government converted them. The named factor is real but secondary — chance plus an individual willing to chase it down is the irreducible combination.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]

practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of William Beveridge for the development of the welfare state.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Beveridge designed the 1909 Labour Exchanges as a young Liberal civil servant.
• At the time: his December 1942 Social Insurance and Allied Services report named the five giants (want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness) and proposed cradle-to-grave social insurance.
• At the time: 300,000 copies were sold; the report shaped wartime public opinion and became Labour’s 1945 manifesto template.
• Over time: family allowances (1945), the National Insurance Act 1946, the National Health Service Act 1946 and the National Assistance Act 1948 all built directly on Beveridge’s blueprint.
• Over time: the contributory model he designed is still used in 21st-century National Insurance.
• Limitation: Beveridge wrote the plan but did not legislate it — a Labour landslide and Bevan’s political skill were also necessary.

[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the National Health Service was created in 1948.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Preconditions: WWII evacuation exposed urban poverty; the Emergency Medical Service nationalised hospitals from 1939; rationing improved working-class diet.
• The Beveridge Report (December 1942) and its 300,000 sales created a public expectation of postwar welfare.
• Trigger: 1945 Labour landslide; Attlee government and Bevan as Minister of Health.
• Response: National Health Service Act 1946; Bevan’s compromise with the BMA in early 1948 (private pay-beds, GPs as contractors).
• 5 July 1948: NHS launches as universal, free at point of use, tax-funded.
• Causal chain: war + communication + government + individual → the world’s first universal health service.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal development with precise dates and named acts.
Secure: Clear development with relevant examples.
Developing: Some development; balance uneven.
Emerging: Lists events without explanation.

practice_questions.text: ‘War has been the main factor in creating the welfare state and the NHS in Britain.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh war against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of war as the main factor:
• WWII evacuation made urban poverty visible to rural Britain; the EMS nationalised hospitals from 1939; rationing established universal entitlement.
• The 1942 Beveridge Report was a wartime commission building on military Keynesianism and the recognition that healthy citizens were a national-security asset.
• The Boer War (1899–1902) had already pushed Liberal reforms 1906–11 by exposing recruit unfitness.

Weighed against communication:
• Booth and Rowntree turned anecdote into evidence by 1901; the Beveridge Report’s 300,000 copies turned policy into popular politics.

Weighed against government:
• The 1945 Labour landslide with a 145-seat majority delivered the National Health Service Act 1946; without parliamentary numbers, Beveridge’s plan would have stayed a paper.

Weighed against the role of the individual:
• Bevan’s deal with the BMA was the make-or-break political move; without his compromise of January-May 1948 the launch would have failed.

Judgement: war repeatedly created the conditions for welfare leaps (1906–11, 1948) by exposing the gap between Britain’s aspirations and its citizens’ health, but war alone did not legislate. The Boer War without Booth/Rowntree, or WWII without Beveridge and Bevan, would not have produced the same leap. War is the necessary trigger, not the sufficient cause.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes wars only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Aneurin Bevan for the development of healthcare in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Bevan as Labour Minister of Health from 1945 designed and steered the National Health Service Act 1946.
• At the time: his compromise with the BMA in early 1948 (consultants kept private pay-beds; GPs remained self-employed contractors) prevented a doctors’ boycott and let the NHS open on 5 July 1948.
• At the time: he resigned in 1951 over the introduction of prescription charges, defending the principle of free at point of use.
• Over time: the NHS structure he created — tripartite (hospitals, GPs, community services), tax-funded, universal — remains the framework of British healthcare today.
• Over time: his model influenced post-war health systems across Europe and the Commonwealth.
• Limitation: significance is partly a product of war and the Beveridge Report — without those preconditions Bevan’s plan would have had no political opening.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and named acts.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the NHS faced opposition before its launch in 1948.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Preconditions: doctors had operated as independent professionals since the 1858 Medical Act; the BMA had blocked or watered down reform attempts since 1911.
• Trigger: the National Health Service Act 1946 proposed salaried hospital consultants and central control of GP contracts.
• The BMA polled members in 1948: an overwhelming majority opposed the plan; January 1948 statement called it ‘so grossly at variance with the essential principles of our profession that it should be rejected absolutely’.
• Bevan negotiated through the spring of 1948: consultants kept private pay-beds; GPs became self-employed contractors paid per registered patient.
• Bevan’s phrase ‘I stuffed their mouths with gold’ captured the financial concessions.
• Causal chain: professional autonomy + financial concern → BMA opposition → political compromise → July 1948 launch.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal development with precise dates and named bodies.
Secure: Clear development with relevant examples.
Developing: Some development; balance uneven.
Emerging: Mentions opposition without explanation.

before.content_html:
War Reshapes the State

The Second World War changed what the British state was thought to be for. Evacuation moved 1.5 million urban children to rural homes from September 1939; middle-class hosts saw the lice, hunger and ragged clothes of city children for the first time. Rationing, far from causing mass hunger, improved working-class diet by guaranteeing protein and vitamins for everyone. The Emergency Medical Service nationalised every hospital bed in 1939 to prepare for air-raid casualties; for the first time central government ran the hospital system. By 1942 the question was no longer whether the state should provide health and welfare, but how.

Key Fact

The Beveridge Report (December 1942) named five ‘giants on the road to reconstruction’: want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. It proposed cradle-to-grave social insurance and free healthcare for all. 300,000 copies sold — popular pressure made postwar welfare politically unavoidable.

The Beveridge Report, December 1942

William Beveridge, the civil servant who had designed the 1909 Labour Exchanges, was asked in 1941 to chair a committee on social insurance. His December 1942 report, Social Insurance and Allied Services, proposed a single contributory scheme covering everyone ‘from cradle to grave’. It assumed three preconditions: family allowances for children, a national health service free at point of use, and full employment. Wartime newspapers serialised it; Penguin produced a cheap paperback. 300,000 copies were sold and the report was studied by ordinary soldiers as well as policymakers. The Conservative-led wartime coalition received it cautiously, but its public profile made any postwar government’s rejection politically impossible.

The 1945 Labour Landslide

In July 1945 the British electorate, while Churchill was still attending the Potsdam Conference, voted Labour into power with 393 seats to the Conservatives’ 197. Clement Attlee became Prime Minister. Aneurin Bevan, the Welsh ex-miner and MP for Ebbw Vale, became Minister of Health. The Education Act 1944 had already raised the school-leaving age and reorganised secondary schools. Family Allowances Act 1945 paid five shillings a week to mothers from the second child. National Insurance Act 1946 replaced the 1911 scheme with universal contributions. National Assistance Act 1948 supported those without insurance contributions. The NHS was the keystone of an interlocking welfare state.

The British Medical Association told members in January 1948 — six months before launch — that Bevan’s plan was ‘so grossly at variance with the essential principles of our profession that it should be rejected absolutely by all practitioners’. Doctors feared becoming salaried civil servants and losing private practice income. Bevan made two compromises: hospital consultants could keep private patients with NHS pay-beds, and GPs would be self-employed contractors paid per registered patient, not state employees. Bevan summarised the deal privately: ‘I stuffed their mouths with gold.’ The BMA voted to accept five weeks before the launch date. Without that compromise there would have been no NHS in July 1948.

5 July 1948: The NHS Opens

On 5 July 1948 the National Health Service Act 1946 came into force. Every British resident was registered with a GP and entitled to free hospital treatment, dental care, eye tests and prescriptions, paid from general taxation. Bevan visited Park Hospital in Manchester (now Trafford General) on the launch day. Demand exceeded every Treasury forecast: 8.5 million pairs of glasses dispensed in the first year, dental treatment for millions who had never seen a dentist, prescription numbers climbing year on year. Bevan resigned from the Cabinet in 1951 after Hugh Gaitskell introduced charges for spectacles and false teeth — a sign that NHS funding was already politically contested in its third year.

Key Fact

The NHS opened on 5 July 1948 as the first universal, tax-funded health service in the world. It was not a national consensus — Bevan won by political calculation against active medical opposition, and the deal preserved private practice inside the new service.

From 1948 the NHS faced what every later generation has called the ‘cost crisis’. Demand grew faster than tax receipts could fund: an ageing population needing more care, expensive new drugs and technologies, rising public expectations, and the long aftershocks of COVID-19 in the 2020s.

Mental health services, historically underfunded, became a political priority from the 2010s. Antibiotic resistance, obesity-related disease and dementia all stretched the budget. The choices the NHS makes in 2026 — rationing, prescription charges, prioritisation by NICE — are direct descendants of Bevan’s 1951 resignation. Free at point of use has remained politically untouchable; how to pay for it has not.

Linking to the Factor Essay

The NHS shows four factors interacting. War: WWII evacuation, EMS nationalisation and military Keynesianism shifted what was thinkable. Communication: the Beveridge Report’s 300,000 copies turned a civil-service paper into mass politics. The role of the individual: Beveridge, Bevan and Attlee each shaped specific outcomes. Government: only a Labour landslide with parliamentary majority could legislate the 1946 Act. The strongest factor essays note that all four were necessary, and that earlier wars (1914–18) without comparable communication or government will produced no equivalent leap.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which government action on public health in 1348 and 1948 were similar or different.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Difference: in 1348 royal government had almost no public health machinery and relied on prayer and street-cleaning orders; in 1948 it created a universal, tax-funded NHS.
• Difference: in 1348 disease was framed as divine punishment; in 1948 it was framed as a public-policy problem to be solved with science and law.
• Similarity: both moments involved central authority responding to mass health crises (Black Death, postwar reconstruction).
• Similarity: both periods relied on individuals to act locally — medieval town councils, modern GPs — because the centre alone could not deliver care.

[4 marks — 2 marks per comparison: 1 for a basic point, 2 for a developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Beveridge Report (1942) for medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: Beveridge named the five giants (want, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness) and proposed cradle-to-grave social insurance plus a free national health service.
• At the time: 300,000 copies sold, building public expectation that any postwar government must legislate welfare.
• Over time: directly shaped the 1945 Family Allowances Act, the 1946 National Insurance Act, the 1946 NHS Act and the 1948 National Assistance Act.
• Over time: the contributory model and universal entitlement remain features of 21st-century British welfare.
• Limitation: Beveridge wrote a plan but did not legislate it — a Labour majority and Bevan’s political skill were necessary to deliver the NHS.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates and named acts.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples covering both periods.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the role of communication has driven medical change across the period.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Preconditions: medieval monastic libraries preserved Hippocrates and Galen but limited their reach to clergy and university-trained physicians.
• The printing press from c1500 spread Vesalius’s Fabrica (1543), Paré’s surgical writings and Harvey’s De Motu Cordis (1628) across Europe within years not generations.
• The Royal Society from 1660 and journals like The Lancet (founded 1823) standardised peer-reviewed reporting; Lister published his antiseptic results there in 1867.
• Booth’s 1889–1903 London survey and Rowntree’s 1901 York study used statistics to translate poverty into a political case.
• The Beveridge Report’s 300,000 copies in 1942 turned a civil-service paper into mass politics.
• Causal chain: each shift in the medium of communication (press, journal, statistics, paperback) widened the audience that could act on medical evidence.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal development across periods with precise dates and named works.
Secure: Clear development with relevant examples.
Developing: Some development; balance uneven.
Emerging: Lists media without explanation.

practice_questions.text: ‘The role of the individual has been the most important factor in the development of British medicine.’ To what extent do you agree? Use examples drawn from across the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should weigh the role of the individual against at least two other factors with a substantiated overall judgement.

In support of the individual as the main factor:
• Vesalius (1543), Paré (1530s–90s) and Harvey (1628) corrected Galen on anatomy, surgery and circulation.
• Jenner (1796) developed vaccination through deliberate experiment.
• Lister (1867) applied germ theory to surgery; Bevan (1948) created the NHS through political compromise.

Weighed against science and technology:
• Vesalius needed printing and improved drawing techniques; Lister needed Pasteur’s germ theory (1860s) and Koch’s microbe identification (1876, 1882). Without these tools the individual’s insight could not have been applied.

Weighed against war:
• Nightingale’s reforms required the Crimean platform; penicillin’s mass production required WWII; the NHS required wartime nationalisation of hospitals through the EMS.

Weighed against government:
• The 1875 Public Health Act, the 1911 National Insurance Act and the 1946 NHS Act were delivered by parliamentary majorities, not individual genius.

Judgement: individuals open doors that no committee opens, but their work only becomes systemic medicine when science gives it tools, war creates pressure, communication spreads it and government legislates it. The individual is necessary but not sufficient — in earlier periods (1348, 1665) individuals existed but the supporting factors did not, so change was limited. The right answer is that the individual is the strongest factor in moments of breakthrough, while government dominates the modern era of system-wide change.

[16 marks plus 4 SPaG]
Mastering: Sustained complex argument weighing the named factor against at least two others with examples from at least two periods and a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear analysis with comparison and a judgement.
Developing: Lists factors without consistent comparative judgement.
Emerging: Describes individuals only, or fails to weigh factors.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the printing press for the development of medicine in Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time: from c1500 the printing press allowed Vesalius’s De Humani Corporis Fabrica (1543), with its detailed anatomical drawings, to circulate across Europe within years rather than centuries.
• At the time: Paré’s surgical writings and Harvey’s De Motu Cordis (1628) reached university libraries and practising physicians at a pace impossible under manuscript copying.
• At the time: it weakened the Church’s monopoly over medical learning by allowing lay readers and Protestant universities to access medical texts.
• Over time: the model of printed peer-reviewed publication carried into journals like The Lancet (1823); Lister’s 1867 antiseptic surgery results spread the same way.
• Over time: mass-circulation paperbacks (e.g. the Beveridge Report’s 300,000 copies in 1942) extended the same logic to public policy.
• Limitation: print only mattered because individuals had something to say — without Vesalius, Harvey or Lister, the press would have spread no medicine.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained significance covering both at the time and over time with precise dates.
Secure: Clear significance with relevant examples.
Developing: Significance attempted but uneven.
Emerging: Brief identification only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how science and technology became the leading factor in nineteenth-century medicine.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Preconditions: by 1800 the Renaissance challenge to Galen, the printing press and the Royal Society had built a culture of experiment.
• Trigger: Pasteur’s germ theory in the 1860s, supported by improved microscopes, gave Britain a usable theory of disease.
• Application: Lister’s 1867 carbolic acid antiseptic surgery in Glasgow, published in The Lancet, demonstrated germ theory’s clinical value.
• Identification: Koch’s isolation of anthrax (1876), tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883) made microbes specific and targetable.
• Industrial backing: Ehrlich’s Salvarsan 606 (1909) and the rise of the pharmaceutical industry turned laboratory science into manufactured medicine.
• Causal chain: theory + tools + industrial scale → science and technology overtook religion and the individual as the lead driver.

[8 marks]
Mastering: Sustained causal development across the century with precise dates and named scientists.
Secure: Clear development with relevant examples.
Developing: Some development; balance uneven.
Emerging: Lists scientists without explanation.

before.content_html:
A Thousand Years on a Single Page

The thematic study asks one large question: why has the pace and direction of medical change varied across British history? The answer lies in the interaction of seven factors — war, religion and superstition, chance, government, communication, science and technology, and the role of the individual. No single factor dominates the whole sweep. Each rises and falls with the period: religion is decisive in the Middle Ages, science in the late nineteenth century, government in the twentieth. The 16-mark factors essay rewards students who can name the named factor, weigh it against two or three others, and make a clear judgement.

Key Fact

One factor tends to dominate each period. Medieval (c1000–c1500): religion. Early modern (c1500–c1750): the role of the individual. Industrial (c1750–c1900): science and technology. Modern (c1900–today): government. Strong essays explain why the lead factor changes and how the others interact.

Mapping the Seven Factors Across the Sweep

Religion and superstition dominates medieval explanations of disease (divine punishment, saints’ cures, the Black Death of 1348 as God’s anger), preserves classical learning through monastic libraries, and limits dissection until the Renaissance. The role of the individual shapes the early-modern disruption: Vesalius (1543), Paré (1530s–90s), Harvey (1628), Sydenham, Hunter, Jenner (1796). Science and technology takes over in the nineteenth century: Pasteur’s germ theory (1860s), Koch (anthrax 1876, TB 1882), Lister’s antiseptic surgery (1867), Snow’s 1854 Broad Street pump, Röntgen’s X-rays (1895). Government dominates the twentieth century: 1875 Public Health Act compulsory, Liberal reforms 1906–11, NHS 1948. War repeatedly accelerates change: Crimean (Nightingale), Boer (Liberal reforms), WWI (transfusion, plastic surgery, X-rays), WWII (penicillin mass production, NHS preconditions). Chance punctuates progress: Paré’s salve, Pasteur’s chicken-cholera culture, Fleming’s mould. Communication spreads everything: the printing press from c1500, the Royal Society from 1660, medical journals like The Lancet, mass-circulation newspapers, the Beveridge Report’s 300,000 copies.

Structuring the 16-Mark Essay

A top-band essay needs a structure that returns to the named factor in every paragraph, not a tour of all seven. The four-paragraph model works:

Introduction: Define the named factor; state your overall judgement (it was/was not the main factor) in one sentence; flag the two other factors you will weigh. Paragraph 1 — the named factor: Two examples from two periods showing the named factor in action. Paragraph 2 — counter-factor A: Strongest rival factor, with one or two examples, and a sentence explicitly comparing it to the named factor. Paragraph 3 — counter-factor B: Second rival factor, again with comparison back to the named factor. Conclusion: A substantiated overall judgement — not a summary. Say which factor mattered most, in which period, and why.

Worked Example: Was Government the main factor in Improving Public Health?

Government in 1348 was almost absent — the Crown ordered fish carts off the road and prayed. In 1665 it ordered shutting up of plague houses but achieved little. By 1848 the first Public Health Act was adoptive (towns chose to opt in) and largely ignored. The 1875 Public Health Act, after the 1867 working-class franchise and germ theory’s spread, was compulsory and comprehensive. The 1948 NHS was decisive. Across this arc, government strengthens as democracy widens and science explains. Counter-factor: science and technology — without Pasteur (1860s), Koch (1882) and Snow (1854) the 1875 Act would have been a shot in the dark. Counter-factor: the role of the individual — Chadwick (1842 report), Snow, Bevan and Beveridge each translated possibilities into laws. Judgement: government became the main factor only after 1875, and only because science and individuals had given it the tools and the case to act.

Key Fact

Three examples, two periods, one judgement. Examiner reports flag every series that strong answers move fluently between periods (e.g. comparing 1348, 1848 and 1948) rather than writing four self-contained mini-essays.

Change, Continuity and Progress

The spec asks not just whether change happened but whether it brought progress. Some change was regression: the loss of Roman aqueducts and bath-houses after c450, replaced by less effective Christian hospitals. Some was sideways: medieval infirmaries served different purposes than classical ones, not necessarily worse. Some was contested: the 1853 Vaccination Act faced organised anti-vaccination resistance, and the 1948 NHS was attacked by the BMA. Strong essays say whose perspective defines progress — what improves life expectancy may not improve patient autonomy; what improves overall health may worsen care for specific groups. The rate of change accelerated unevenly: medieval slow, Renaissance start-stop, nineteenth-century rapid, twentieth-century explosive.

AQA principal examiner reports flag the same mistakes every series. Do not write in the first person or as a diary entry — that prevents AO2 analytical marks. Do not list factors without weighing them; listing all seven is not analysis. Do not stay in one period — the 16-mark essay requires examples from at least two periods.

Do not give vague figures — ‘a lot of soldiers’ is not 40%; ‘many people’ is not 30.7% of Londoners. Use the named individuals from the spec (Vesalius, Harvey, Paré, Hunter, Jenner, Pasteur, Koch, Ehrlich, Simpson, Lister, Snow, Chadwick, Nightingale, Booth, Rowntree, Beveridge, Bevan, Fleming, Florey, Chain) by name and date. Reach a substantiated overall judgement — the conclusion is what separates the top band from the rest.
